title: Lahore Is Putting Hindu, Sikh and Jain Names Back on Its Streets. For the Diaspora, It Feels Like a Door Reopening.
excerpt: Pakistan’s Punjab government has restored nine pre-Partition street names in Lahore — including Krishan Nagar, Dharampura and Jain Mandir Chowk — in a heritage push that has stirred memories across the border.
body:
Nearly eight decades after Partition carved the subcontinent apart, Lahore is reclaiming the names its residents never actually stopped using. Islampura is once again Krishan Nagar. Babri Masjid Chowk has reverted to Jain Mandir Chowk. Mustafaabad is Dharampura again. And Sunnat Nagar is now, officially, Sant Nagar.

The renaming — nine locations so far — is the centrepiece of a heritage restoration drive approved by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s cabinet. New signboards bearing the older names have already appeared across the city over the past two months, quietly reversing decades of systematic erasure that followed Partition.

## A City That Remembered Anyway

For Lahoris, the names never truly disappeared. “The people still call them by the old names,” Kamran Lashari, former director-general of the Walled City of Lahore and secretary of the Lahore Heritage Foundation, told *The Print*. Tea sellers, shopkeepers, rickshaw drivers and residents kept the pre-1947 names alive in everyday conversation, regardless of what the signboards said.

Lakshmi Chowk, once officially renamed Maulana Zafar Ali Khan Chowk, was always Lakshmi Chowk. Davis Road, which had become Sir Aga Khan Road, was still Davis Road to anyone giving directions. Lawrence Gardens — known for years as Bagh-e-Jinnah — is now reclaiming its colonial-era association.

Lashari said the effort deliberately embraces Lahore’s layered identity. “Whether it is Christian, Sikh, Hindu or Parsi, it doesn’t matter,” he said. The restoration work also extends to churches and Sikh-era structures connected to Maharaja Ranjit Singh’s empire. At Lahore Fort, authorities have restored a painting of Princess Bamba Sutherland, the last descendant of the Sikh royal family.

## The Partition Wound That Never Fully Closed

Lahore sits barely 50 kilometres from Amritsar. Before 1947, the two cities were part of the same cultural ecosystem — Punjabis across faiths shared bazaars, colleges, gardens, akharas, temples, gurdwaras and shrines. Partition destroyed that overnight. The majority of Hindu and Sikh families fled or were driven out during the communal violence that accompanied independence. In the decades that followed, names linked to Hindu, Sikh or British history were gradually replaced with Islamic or Pakistani nationalist ones.

The reversal is not purely symbolic. It is also being paired with physical restoration of heritage structures. Lahore is home to more than 100 recognised heritage sites, and work is underway on dozens of colonial-era buildings.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For the millions of Punjabi families — in India, the UK, Canada, the United States — whose grandparents or great-grandparents once walked these streets, the move carries an emotional weight that policy announcements rarely do. The names Krishan Nagar and Dharampura are not just geographic labels; they are fragments of family memory, handed down through generations of oral history.

Nawaz Sharif has also proposed restoring Lahore’s historic cricket grounds and the old wrestling arena at Minto Park — now called Greater Iqbal Park — which produced legends on both sides of the border. Before Partition, the grounds turned out generations of cricketers, including Pakistan’s Inzamam-ul-Haq and India’s Lala Amarnath. The park’s demolished akhara once hosted bouts involving legendary wrestlers such as Gama Pehalwan and Imam Bakhsh.

## A Complicated Legacy

The restoration is not without critics. Pakistan’s minority population has shrunk from roughly 20 per cent at Partition to around 3.5 per cent today, and rights groups have pointed out that renaming streets does not address the persecution, forced conversions and institutional discrimination that minorities continue to face.

Earlier attempts to honour Lahore’s Sikh heritage — including an effort to install a statue of Maharaja Ranjit Singh — faced vandalism. But Lashari said the atmosphere has become more open in recent years.

For now, though, the signboards are changing. And for families on both sides of the Wagah border — and across the diaspora — Lahore sounds a little more like home.
